items.title: Test whether report questions preserve every condition
items.summary: A report assistant is only useful if it follows every part of a question. This paper shows that AI models can pick the wrong table row or overlook one requirement when a question asks for several things at once. The researchers help the model notice row and column structure and train it in stages on increasingly involved questions. They test published research datasets, including tables resembling financial reports, rather than your spreadsheets or calculations. A practical trial would ask questions combining a month, account and amount, then check each requirement separately instead of accepting an answer merely because it sounds reasonable.
items.why_it_matters: Branding-Report-Automation and Daily-Position-Automation both depend on structured figures. A focused condition-by-condition test could expose answers that look reasonable while using the wrong row, column or filter.
items.application_example: Create a synthetic monthly sales table with regions, product families, invoice dates and net amounts. Ask, “Which North-region products sold after 15 August and exceeded ₹50,000 after returns?” Record whether the system identifies the correct header, applies all four conditions and cites the supporting cells. Include near-miss rows that satisfy three conditions so a reviewer can see whether one condition was silently dropped. Keep the existing arithmetic and reconciliation logic as the authority.
items.evidence_label: peer-reviewed paper: Compositional Condition Question Answering in Tabular Understanding; proposed application not tested
guidance: Where: Place the experiment after a synthetic report table is produced, before any natural-language answer is shown to an operator.
Try: Write twenty questions combining two to four requirements, with almost-correct rows designed to reveal when one requirement was skipped.
Benefit: The test can reveal convincing answers based on the wrong cells before table question answering is considered for routine reporting.
Effort: Allow one day to prepare labelled tables and a small scoring script; adapting the paper's training method would be substantially larger work.
Check: Inspect the selected cells and each requirement, then compare the answer with an ordinary spreadsheet formula and reject unsupported responses.

items.title: Reuse reviewed browser workflows without treating them as guarantees
items.summary: A browser assistant may complete repeated tasks more consistently when it can reuse a checklist learned from past successful steps. This paper turns earlier web journeys into reusable instructions, either before work begins or while the assistant gains experience. On two research test sets, this helped agents finish more tasks and, in one set, use fewer steps when successful. A learned checklist still needs care because websites, permissions and records change. For GHADC, a small trial could match a new fictional request with an approved earlier journey, then check the visible page and record status after every important action.
items.why_it_matters: GHADC contains browser workflows, roles and state transitions. Reusing successful patterns may reduce repeated planning, while explicit state checks preserve the project’s need for understandable approval behavior.
items.application_example: In a test copy of a portal, record successful journeys for submitting, reviewing and rejecting fictional applications. When given a new “submit and obtain manager review” task, retrieve the closest reviewed workflow. Before each click, confirm the page, role and record identifier; after each click, confirm the expected status. Deliberately rename one button and remove one permission. The agent should stop and report the mismatch instead of improvising an approval.
items.evidence_label: peer-reviewed paper: Agent Workflow Memory; proposed application not tested
guidance: Where: Use a disposable GHADC test environment containing fictional accounts and records, starting with one complete approval journey.
Try: Record five reviewed browser journeys, turn them into reusable checklists, and compare new tasks with and without a matching checklist.
Benefit: Reused routines may shorten repeated browser tasks and make the intended sequence easier for a developer to inspect.
Effort: Allow two days for a narrow prototype, including page-status checks and activity records; live permissions and recovery would require separate design.
Check: Change labels, roles and record states deliberately; require safe stopping whenever the page no longer matches the workflow's assumptions.

items.title: Give coding agents a fixed path from reproduction to validation
items.summary: A coding assistant is easier to review when it follows a clear repair sequence. PatchPilot uses five steps: reproduce the bug, find the responsible code, prepare a change, run checks and improve the change if needed. The researchers evaluate this sequence on SWE-bench, a collection of real software issues used for research. Those results do not show that the assistant can safely change this portfolio’s accounting or reporting code. A useful trial would therefore focus on one invented defect with a known correct result, keep a record from every step and leave the final decision to a person.
items.why_it_matters: The portfolio includes several Python automations where a plausible patch could alter figures. A staged repair record would make reproduction evidence, changed files and validation results easier to review.
items.application_example: Introduce a synthetic bug in a copy of a parser so a continuation row is counted twice. Give the agent the failure description and fixture. Require it to reproduce the wrong total, identify the narrow parsing branch, propose a patch, run the known regression suite and refine only if a test fails. The final report should show the original failure, exact diff and test evidence. A person should decide whether the patch is acceptable; nothing should be merged automatically.
items.evidence_label: peer-reviewed paper: PatchPilot: A Cost-Efficient Software Engineering Agent with Early Attempts on Formal Verification; proposed application not tested
guidance: Where: Run the trial on a temporary branch with synthetic documents and an intentionally introduced parsing defect.
Try: Enforce the paper's five stages and save one concise artifact from each stage for later human review.
Benefit: A fixed repair sequence can make agent work easier to audit and may reduce aimless exploration on well-specified bugs.
Effort: Allow half a day if checks and example files already exist; weak coverage of existing behavior must improve before meaningful evaluation.
Check: Confirm the original failure reproduces, the smallest responsible code changed, and both targeted and surrounding calculation tests pass.

items.title: Generate a failing test from an issue before trusting a patch
items.summary: A clear bug report could help produce the missing test before anyone changes the code. Otter reads a written software issue, creates a candidate test and uses that test to judge whether a proposed repair addresses the reported behavior. The researchers evaluate this approach on tasks drawn from software repositories. This separation matters because a repair can pass the old tests while still missing the exact problem reported by a user. A generated test may also misunderstand the report. For this portfolio, a developer should inspect each candidate, confirm it fails before the repair and confirm it passes afterward for the intended reason.
items.why_it_matters: TCPL-Data-Entry and the document automations have edge cases that can be described by operators. Turning those descriptions into reviewable regression-test candidates could shorten the path from report to reproducible evidence.
items.application_example: Write a fictional issue: “When the uploaded workbook contains a blank optional column before Amount, the preview moves every later value one column left.” Ask the system for a minimal workbook fixture and test. A developer checks that the fixture actually represents the report, that the test fails on the known defect, and that a correct fix passes. Add a neighbouring case with no blank column to ensure the candidate test does not permit a regression in normal imports.
items.evidence_label: peer-reviewed paper: Otter: Generating Tests from Issues to Validate SWE Patches; proposed application not tested
guidance: Where: Insert the experiment between a well-specified synthetic bug report and any attempt to change the importer code.
Try: Generate tests for five historical-style edge cases, then have a developer label each test valid, invalid or incomplete.
Benefit: Useful candidates could make vague failures reproducible sooner and give patch review a concrete before-and-after condition.
Effort: Allow one day to prepare precise issues and example files; expect manual correction when a generated check misunderstands the requirement.
Check: Every accepted test must fail before the fix, pass afterward, protect a neighbouring behavior and avoid depending on private data.

items.title: Explore recommendations that preserve identity and descriptive variety
items.summary: A recommendation can become more personal when the system remembers patterns in what each person liked, rather than relying only on written product descriptions. This paper groups similar user and item histories, gives each group a special internal label and teaches a language model to use those labels when making recommendations. The researchers report results on established recommendation tasks, not on a small coffee catalogue. A user-facing trial for forty-degrees could compare this method with a simple ratings-based approach. Customers would see three suggestions and plain reasons based only on their own recorded preferences and the coffee descriptions held by the application.
items.why_it_matters: forty-degrees combines a small product interface with preference learning. This paper offers a concrete way to investigate whether interaction history adds useful distinctions beyond free-text coffee descriptions.
items.application_example: Build a separate prototype containing thirty fictional coffees, attributes such as roast and acidity, and synthetic rating histories for ten customers. After a customer rates five coffees, show three suggestions with plain reasons such as “similar roast to two coffees you rated highly.” Compare them with a non-LLM collaborative-filtering baseline. Let the customer hide or correct a preference and recalculate the list. Never expose learned tokens or another customer’s history in the interface.
items.evidence_label: peer-reviewed paper: Improving LLMs for Recommendation with Out-Of-Vocabulary Tokens; user product concept not tested
guidance: Where: Add a separate experimental recommendation page using fictional catalogue entries and synthetic customer histories.
Try: Compare popular choices, a simple ratings-based method and the paper-inspired method using the same ratings hidden for checking.
Benefit: The study can show whether richer identity and interaction signals improve discovery enough to justify added model complexity.
Effort: Allow several days for a small private experiment; adding internal labels and retraining a model exceeds a basic interface prototype.
Check: Measure held-out ranking quality, inspect recommendation diversity and verify every displayed reason against attributes and ratings actually stored.

items.title: Probe whether a document assistant follows corrupted retrieved evidence
items.summary: A report assistant needs to choose trustworthy source material before it writes an answer. This paper studies systems that first find relevant passages and then ask a language model to answer from them. It shows how deliberately misleading material can influence answers in specialist subject areas. The study does not measure your reports, permissions or document process, but it highlights a useful test. Give a trial assistant an approved report, an old draft and a misleading note. Then check whether it uses the approved source, links each claim to the right passage and says it cannot answer when dependable evidence is missing.
items.why_it_matters: A future Branding-Report-Automation question box would be useful only if its sources are controlled and its claims remain traceable. This paper motivates testing the retrieval boundary before evaluating answer fluency.
items.application_example: Prepare three fictional monthly reports. One approved report states that net sales were ₹900,000; an older draft says ₹960,000; a planted note claims ₹1.2 million. Ask for net sales and the reason for the change. Record which passages were retrieved, whether the approved version outranks the others, and whether the answer cites the exact report. Then remove the approved passage: the assistant should say the approved documents do not establish an answer.
items.evidence_label: peer-reviewed paper: On the Vulnerability of Applying Retrieval-Augmented Generation within Knowledge-Intensive Application Domains; proposed application not tested
guidance: Where: Test the retrieval layer of an isolated report assistant containing only synthetic approved, stale and deliberately misleading documents.
Try: Build twenty questions with conflicting passages and vary source status, duplication and wording while keeping the correct evidence fixed.
Benefit: The exercise can expose whether source controls and citations fail before a polished answer reaches a report reader.
Effort: Allow one to two days for a compact set of deliberately difficult examples and source-selection records; live access controls require separate engineering.
Check: Require links to approved passages, verify each claim manually and require the assistant to decline when dependable evidence is missing or contradictory.

items.title: Evaluate computer agents with realistic state and recovery checks
items.summary: Before allowing an AI assistant to operate a computer, you need repeatable tasks that show what it can and cannot do. Windows Agent Arena supplies more than 150 such tasks involving planning, reading screens and using desktop applications. The researchers can reset and run many tests in parallel. Their best tested agent completed far fewer tasks than people, so the paper also gives a clear reason to start cautiously. Its results do not predict performance in your applications. The useful idea is to define exact starting points and expected end results for read-only spreadsheet or browser tasks, then repeat them and inspect every failure.
items.why_it_matters: The portfolio includes Windows-based data-entry and browser workflows. A resettable task suite would make claims about computer-use agents measurable before considering any operational integration.
items.application_example: Create a disposable Windows profile with a fictional workbook and local test portal. Define tasks such as opening the correct sheet, locating a mismatched total, and navigating to a draft request without submitting it. Save a clean snapshot before each run and score final state from workbook cells and page status. Include interruptions such as a dialog box or moved shortcut. Any attempt to submit, post or alter the source fixture should fail the task immediately.
items.evidence_label: peer-reviewed paper: Windows Agent Arena: Evaluating Multi-Modal OS Agents at Scale; proposed application not tested
guidance: Where: Use a disposable Windows account and local example files, with network and editing permissions restricted to the test environment.
Try: Define ten read-only tasks, exact starting snapshots and machine-checkable end states, then repeat each task several times.
Benefit: Repeatable scoring can replace impressive demonstrations with evidence about reliability, recovery and unwanted actions on representative workflows.
Effort: Allow two days for the first environment and task set; stable reset automation may take longer than the agent integration.
Check: Score both intended results and forbidden changes, inspect the steps from failed runs and repeat from identical starting copies to measure consistency.
